statement: Benching Dunsparce under Risky Ruins puts 20 damage on your own Pokémon, which Munkidori can then move onto the opponent's board each turn.
quote: It also can be really strong with the risky runes, allowing you to bench it, bench dun sparks under risky runes to put 20 damage on it and then you can use monkey dory and move that 20 damage every single turn to your opponent's side of the board.

statement: In the mirror, delay the first big attack until enough spread damage is banked, because attacking early exposes you to Crushing Hammer and Unfair Stamp counterplay.
quote: kind of want to wait until you accumulate up enough damage on their board to just maybe like take out all their draco all their threats before you go in because if you go in too early of course they could use something like the crushing hammers and the unfair stamp and kind of put you really far behind

statement: Removing the opponent's Darkness Energy with Crushing Hammer stops their Munkidori from moving the damage back.
quote: This can be combined with also crushing hammer on their monkey dory dark energy or something too.

statement: With only two Night Stretcher the card feels like a scarce resource; with three it functions as a consistency card.
quote: when you have two, you have to worry about, am I going to run out of night stretchers?

statement: In the mirror, Ultra Balls accumulate unused (partly because of item lock), which justified cutting to three.
quote: in the mirror matches, I would get to the end of the game and I kind of have like two or three of my Ultra Balls left

statement: Outside the mirror Ultra Ball is used far more, so the three-count costs more there; do not burn them without value.
quote: is a little bit less good to only play three ultra ball. You do find yourself using them a lot more since you're never item locked

statement: A third Darkness Energy makes it easier to get Munkidori online early while under Budew item lock.
quote: Having access to dark energy early allows you to set up Monkey Dory while you're being vued a little bit easier.

statement: Winning the early Budew item-lock exchange is very often decisive in the mirror.
quote: And winning this itchy pollen war in the mirror match to start out the game is just so so important a lot of the time.

statement: Do not be the first player to commit to attacking while your board is still underdeveloped.
quote: Uh, you don't want to be the first one to go in with an underdeveloped board.

statement: Multiple Munkidori are a comeback tool from a weak board.
quote: Setting up multiple monkey dories can be really strong.

statement: Against Zoroark, attacking early with Dragapult is strong when the opponent cannot answer with a Knock Out that turn.
quote: one of the best ways that Dragult can win this matchup is by going really aggressive with a Dragapult if the Zorg player isn't going to have a response knockout on the turn you go in

statement: Before attacking, check whether the opponent's Munkidori plus Phantom Dive answers your board; that can make the aggressive line lose.
quote: However, if I do this, he can just use his monkey dory, move 30 to my Draco on the bench, and then phantom dive me back.

statement: When the opponent attacks into your Dragapult, retreating it and switching to Munkidori damage-moving plus Budew lock can be stronger than continuing to attack.
quote: I think I was able to get to a point where he hits into my Dragapult one turn and then I kind of just retreat it and start moving damage with Monkey Dory using Pedu

statement: Going first in the mirror, playing Risky Ruins punishes the opponent's benched Budew with 20 damage, so your own Budew can then Knock it Out.
quote: Putting risky runes down and mirror going first is really good because generally because it means if your opponent benches bed then their bed takes 20.

statement: In the Bronzong/Lopunny matchup, Knocking Out the Bronzong was the worst of the three targets considered.
quote: But killing the bronzong here would be the worst play.

statement: Knocking Out Dusclops protected both his Drakloak and his Fezandipiti ex from being Knocked Out the following turn.
quote: if I knock out the dusk wops in my drake is fairly likely to survive to the next turn

statement: Fezandipiti ex is one of the best attackers in the Bronzong/Lopunny matchup because Cruel Arrow snipes and is not shut off by Bronzong.
quote: Fasendipity is one of the best attackers in this matchup.

statement: Play so that the opponent's remaining Boss's Orders cannot win on the spot; count how many they have used.
quote: orders is not really something I want to do.

statement: With limited disruption left, check the opponent for the resource they are most likely to miss (Energy) rather than the one they can more easily find.
quote: I thought it'd be better to try to check her for energy

statement: Count the opponent's remaining outs (cards left in deck) before choosing between two disruption lines.
quote: her chances of actually being able to draw an energy are still

statement: Recovering a Darkness Energy in advance protects against a Crushing Hammer chain that would otherwise lock Munkidori out of the game.
quote: think I probably should have played a night stretcher the turn before to put one of my dark energies from my discard pile back in my hand.
notes: Hedrick states this as his own mistake.

statement: Hedrick judges his actual play in that position inferior to the alternative he demonstrates (Knocking Out Torchic and Budew to threaten a win next turn).
quote: So, should have done this, but instead I don't.
notes: Self-identified mistake; the alternative is explained in the surrounding minutes.

statement: Passing with Fezandipiti ex active while building Energy can be correct when the opponent has spent most of their gust effects.
quote: passed with the fez in that active set up more energy on my board.

statement: Against the Rabsca version of Alakazam, small disruption is disproportionately effective because their board space and draw are strained.
quote: their deck just can kind of crumble, can kind of fall apart uh to the littlest things

statement: Special Red Card plus Knocking Out their draw Pokémon can leave board-constrained decks with no draw.
quote: Sometimes you can just like red card and kill it a don sparse.

statement: Against Zoroark, a slow start is very hard to recover from, so pressure early.
quote: it's really really hard to get enough cards to see enough cards to put yourself in a spot where you can actually turn the game around

statement: In the Worlds final game 2, Hedrick says the alternative line (Special Red Card, Lillie's Determination, Knock Out Dunsparce and Phantom Dive) may have been better than the deck-out line he chose.
quote: I think it's like reasonable for me also to have just tried to play the red card, play the lily, um take out a Dun Sparse and Phantom dive through his active that turn
notes: Self-doubt about his own winning line: explicitly disputed.

statement: Infer the opponent's hand by asking which cards they would have played if they held them.
quote: you can just ask yourself like if my opponent had this card would they have played it?

statement: Track the opponent's exact hand size and the cards you saw them search, and use that to evaluate your options.
quote: So Diego has five cards left and we know one of them is Kadabra.

statement: Farah judges the aggressive turn-2 Dragon Headbutt as high upside and hard to punish, given the read on the opponent's hand.
quote: So, there's a lot of upside from Andrew's play and it's very unlikely Diego gets to punish

statement: Knocking Out Fezandipiti ex avoids giving the opponent the Flip the Script draw that a different Knock Out would trigger.
quote: by hitting the Fez, you also don't trigger Flip the Script.

statement: Farah states that in game 1 of the final Hedrick missed a winning line on the penultimate turn.
quote: it's from the penultimate turn of game one where Andrew actually did miss a checkmate
notes: Farah does not give the line; he leaves it as an exercise. Unresolved.

statement: Dragapult's spread damage and hand disruption are the two things Alakazam struggles with.
quote: Dragapult's spread damage and hand disruption are both difficult obstacles for Alakazam.

statement: Alakazam's counter-cards to Dragapult are Battle Cage (protects the Bench), Eri (stops Special Red Card or Unfair Stamp) and Genesect (a more reliable answer to Unfair Stamp).
quote: Battle Cage can protect the Bench, as long as Dragapult doesn't find one of their two Stadiums. Eri can stop Special Red Card or Unfair Stamp , while Genesect is a more reliable counter to Unfair Stamp.
notes: Two Stadiums in the Dragapult list are the answer to Battle Cage.

statement: Dragapult was 43% of the Worlds 2026 field, per Manley.
quote: due to the extremely high presence of Dragapult (43% of the field)
notes: Limitless day-2 statistics give 29.37% of day 2 (42 of 143 decks); the 43% figure is Manley's and its denominator is unstated.

statement: After Hedrick won LA Regionals, Crushing Hammer became the default inclusion in Dragapult lists, with players cutting Rare Candy and tech cards for it.
quote: When Andrew Hedrick won the Los Angeles Regionals, Crushing Hammer quickly became the default inclusion in Dragapult ex lists.
notes: Smart argues the Crushing Hammer build is weaker as the format widens: a dissenting view.

statement: In day 2 of Worlds 2026, Dragapult was the most represented deck with 42 of 143 decks (29.37%).
quote: 1 Dragapult 42 29.37% 647
notes: Aggregate tournament data, used only to prioritise matchups. Alakazam 16 (11.19%), N's Zoroark 12 (8.39%), Basic Box 18 (12.59%), Slowking 11 (7.69%).
